posts.title: What Happens When You Die? What the Bible Really Teaches
posts.author: Jack Thompson
posts.seoTitle: What Happens When You Die? What the Bible Really Says
posts.metaDesc: What happens when you die according to the Bible? A gentle, Scripture based look at death, the resurrection, and the hope of seeing our loved ones again.
posts.excerpt: A gentle look at death, the resurrection, and the hope of seeing our loved ones again.
body: The phone call came late at night. Or maybe it was a slow goodbye in a hospital room, holding a hand that grew quieter and then finally still. If you have lost someone you love, you know the questions that come afterward, often in the middle of the night. Where are they now? Can they see me? Are they at peace? Will I ever hold them again?

At the start of November, many families feel these questions even more deeply. Toussaint and the days around it bring candles, cemetery visits, flowers on graves, and memories of mothers, fathers, grandparents, and children who are gone. For many Haitian families, it is a season when the line between the living and the dead can feel especially thin.

The Bible does not leave us guessing about any of this. It speaks about death honestly, without pretending it is anything less than an enemy. And it speaks about hope even more boldly, with promises that reach all the way to resurrection morning. In this article we will look carefully at what Scripture actually teaches, answer the passages people most often ask about, and see why this teaching brings so much comfort to grieving hearts.
## The short answer

The Bible teaches that when a person dies, they rest unconscious in the grave, much like a deep and dreamless sleep, until Jesus returns and raises them to life. The faithful do not drift as spirits, wander between worlds, or watch from somewhere unseen. Their next conscious moment will be hearing the voice of Jesus calling them home at the resurrection (John 5:28 to 29, 1 Thessalonians 4:16).

This is the official teaching of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, and it rests on a consistent reading of Scripture from Genesis to Revelation rather than on one or two verses. Christians from several traditions have held this understanding throughout history. Let us walk through why, starting at the very beginning.
## How God made us helps explain death
To understand what happens at death, it helps to start with how God created life in the first place. The Creation story gives us a simple and beautiful picture of what a human being is.
> "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Genesis 2:7, KJV

Notice the formula in this verse. God took dust from the ground, added the breath of life, and the result was a living soul. Adam did not receive a soul as a separate part that was placed inside his body. He became a soul. Throughout the Old Testament, the word "soul" usually means the whole living person, which is why Scripture can speak of a certain number of "souls" traveling with Jacob to Egypt, meaning people.

Death simply reverses what happened at Creation. "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7). The Hebrew word for spirit in this verse, ruach, also means breath or wind. Job uses it the same way when he says "the spirit of God is in my nostrils" (Job 27:3), clearly speaking about his breath.

So at death, the body returns to the dust, and the breath of life that God gave returns to Him. What returns to God is not a conscious ghost carrying the person's thoughts, but the life force He loaned. The person rests, and God holds every detail of who they were safely in His care until the day He gives them life again.
## What the Bible says about the dead

When we read the passages that speak directly about the condition of the dead, a clear and consistent picture appears. These verses come from different writers across many centuries, yet they say the same thing in plain language.

Ecclesiastes states it most directly: "For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5). The writer goes on to say that the dead no longer have any part in anything that happens "under the sun" (Ecclesiastes 9:6). Their love, their worries, and their plans have all come to rest. They are not watching events unfold on earth or carrying the weight of what happens to the family they left behind.

The Psalms describe the same reality. "His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish" (Psalm 146:4). Another psalm says, "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence" (Psalm 115:17). If the faithful went straight to heaven at death, we would expect the psalmist to describe them praising God more fully than ever. Instead, he describes the grave as a place of silence and rest.

The New Testament adds an important truth about immortality. Paul writes that God "only hath immortality" (1 Timothy 6:16). In other words, human beings are not naturally immortal. Immortality is a gift that God gives to the redeemed at the resurrection, when "this mortal must put on immortality" (1 Corinthians 15:53). It is not something we carry inside us by nature.

Even the greatest heroes of faith are still waiting for that day. King David, called a man after God's own heart (1 Samuel 13:14), died about a thousand years before Christ. Yet on the day of Pentecost, Peter told the crowd in Jerusalem, "David is not ascended into the heavens" (Acts 2:34). David's tomb was still with them, and David himself was resting until the resurrection.
## Jesus called death a sleep

Perhaps the clearest teaching about death comes from Jesus Himself. When His dear friend Lazarus died, Jesus told His disciples, "Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep" (John 11:11). The disciples misunderstood and thought Lazarus was simply resting from illness, so Jesus told them plainly, "Lazarus is dead" (John 11:14).

That was the picture Jesus chose to describe death, and He chose it carefully. Sleep is real, and it involves no awareness of passing time. But sleep is not the end. You lie down at night expecting to wake up in the morning. For those who belong to Jesus, death is a sleep that will end with the brightest morning the world has ever seen.

What is striking about the story of Lazarus is what Lazarus did not say. He lay in the tomb for four days, long enough that his sisters worried about the smell. If he had been in heaven during those days, he would have had the greatest story ever told, and surely someone would have written it down. Yet Scripture records no report from him about the afterlife, because there was nothing to report. He was asleep until Jesus called his name.

The rest of the New Testament uses this same language again and again. When Stephen became the first Christian martyr, Luke writes that "he fell asleep" (Acts 7:60). Paul comforts believers about loved ones "which are asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). And centuries earlier, the prophet Daniel described the dead as those who "sleep in the dust of the earth" and who "shall awake" (Daniel 12:2). The Bible speaks with one voice on this.
## The great hope: resurrection morning

If death were the whole story, this would be a very sad article. It is not. The Bible's answer to death is not a shadowy, ghostly afterlife. It is a resurrection, with a real body, a real reunion with the people we love, and a real face to face meeting with Jesus.

> "For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air." 1 Thessalonians 4:16 to 17, KJV

Read those words slowly, especially the phrase "together with them." Paul wrote this letter to believers who were grieving the loss of loved ones, so that they would "sorrow not, even as others which have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Christians still grieve, and our tears are real. But we grieve with a reunion in view, the way you might cry at an airport while already looking forward to the day you will be together again.

Paul describes the moment of resurrection in 1 Corinthians 15. "In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump... the dead shall be raised incorruptible" (verse 52). Our weak and mortal bodies will "put on immortality" (verse 53), and the whole church will sing a song of victory: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" (verse 55). Death, which has taken so much from so many, will finally lose.

Jesus made this promise personal when He stood outside the tomb of Lazarus. "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live" (John 11:25). That same hope carried believers long before Jesus came. Job, in the middle of terrible suffering, declared, "I know that my redeemer liveth," and looked forward to seeing God "in my flesh" (Job 19:25 to 26). The hope of the resurrection runs through the whole Bible.
## Why this teaching brings comfort

Some people worry at first that the idea of death as a sleep sounds cold or sad. In practice, many grieving families find it deeply freeing, once they understand what it means for the people they love.

First, it means your loved one is not suffering or waiting anxiously somewhere. For the person who dies trusting in Jesus, no time passes at all. They close their eyes in death, and their very next awareness will be resurrection morning, seeing Jesus coming in glory. This is why Paul could say he wanted to "depart, and to be with Christ" (Philippians 1:23). From the believer's point of view, death is followed immediately by Christ's appearing, even if centuries pass on earth.

Second, it means your loved one is not watching your pain. Many people imagine a mother in heaven seeing her children struggle, or a grandfather watching the family argue and drift apart. If that were true, heaven would be a place of constant heartbreak. The Bible spares the dead that grief. They rest in peace, untouched by sorrow, until the day God wipes away every tear from every eye (Revelation 21:4).

Third, it means you do not need to fear the dead. They cannot harm you, haunt you, punish you, or demand anything from you. They are not angry spirits that must be calmed or pleased. They are safe in God's memory, and nothing about who they were is lost to Him. When the resurrection comes, God will restore them fully.
![A person holding a lit candle among rows of candles](1680546852052-17874e3fa110)
## A word to Haitian families

Many of us grew up in homes where the dead never felt far away. We heard that spirits visit in dreams, that they need to be fed or honored, or that they can bring blessing or trouble to the living depending on how they are treated. Around Fèt Gede in early November, these beliefs become especially visible across Haiti and throughout the diaspora, from Port au Prince to Miami to here in Texas.

These traditions often grow out of real love for those who have died and a deep longing to stay connected to them. That longing is not wrong. It is a sign of how much our families matter to us, and God Himself placed that love in our hearts. He understands it better than anyone.

But Scripture gives a clear and loving warning. God told Israel not to consult mediums or anyone who seeks to speak with the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10 to 12). The prophet Isaiah asks a searching question: "should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?" (Isaiah 8:19). Since the Bible teaches that the dead know nothing, any voice, dream, or presence that claims to be a departed loved one cannot truly be them. The Bible warns that spiritual deception is real, and that the enemy can even disguise himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14).

The good news here is freedom. You do not owe the dead anything, and you do not have to keep them happy or protect yourself from them. Jesus says He holds "the keys of hell and of death" (Revelation 1:18), which means no power in the spirit world has the final word over your family. Your loved ones who trusted Him are in His hands, and so are you. You can honor their memory with gratitude, stories, and love, while placing your trust fully in the living God.
## Questions people ask

Whenever this topic is discussed, a few passages are often raised as evidence that the dead are conscious. These are sincere questions that deserve careful answers. Here is how Adventists understand each one in the light of the whole Bible.
### What about the thief on the cross?

In Luke 23:43, Jesus says to the repentant thief, "Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." The original Greek manuscripts had no punctuation, so translators must decide where to place the comma. The verse can be read as, "I say unto thee today, you will be with me in paradise," an emphatic promise given on the darkest day of Jesus' life. This reading fits the rest of Scripture well. On Sunday morning, after His resurrection, Jesus told Mary, "I am not yet ascended to my Father" (John 20:17). Jesus Himself did not go to paradise that Friday, so the thief could not have joined Him there that day. The promise was certain, and its fulfillment comes at the resurrection.
### Doesn't Paul say to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord?

In 2 Corinthians 5:8, Paul expresses his longing to be with Christ. But the verses just before (2 Corinthians 5:1 to 4) explain what he is longing for. He describes groaning to be "clothed upon" with a new, heavenly body, not to be "unclothed" as a bodiless spirit. Elsewhere Paul is clear that his reward will come "at that day," when Jesus appears (2 Timothy 4:8). Because no time passes for those who rest in death, the believer who dies moves, from their own point of view, directly into the presence of the Lord at His coming.
### What about the rich man and Lazarus?

Luke 16:19 to 31 is a parable, part of a series of stories Jesus told in Luke 15 and 16 to teach spiritual lessons. If we read it literally, it would mean that heaven and hell are close enough for people to talk across, and that a drop of water on the tongue could ease a soul in flames. Jesus used a story familiar to His listeners to make one central point: our choices in this life matter eternally, and Scripture is enough to lead us to repentance (Luke 16:31). The parable was never meant to be a map of the afterlife.
### Can our loved ones see us from heaven?

According to Ecclesiastes 9:5 to 6, the dead know nothing and have no part in what happens on earth. That may feel hard to hear at first, especially if you have found comfort in imagining a loved one watching over you. But it means they are spared the sorrow of watching us suffer, struggle, or grieve. They are resting in peace, and the joy of seeing one another again is waiting for resurrection day, when it will be complete and never end.
![Bright sun shining over a misty rural field](1764618979767-4ab5e3d2a509)
## Reflection questions

Take some quiet time with these questions, perhaps with your Bible open beside you. Begin by asking which promise about the resurrection speaks most to your heart right now, and why it matters so much to you. Then consider how knowing that your loved one is resting, not watching, might change the way you carry your grief. Finally, ask God honestly whether there is any fear about death or the dead that He wants to lift from you today.
## A word of encouragement

If you are grieving, your tears are not a sign of weak faith. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, even though He knew He would raise him to life just minutes later (John 11:35). He was moved by the sorrow of the people around Him, and He is moved by yours too. You never grieve alone.

And remember this: Jesus has already walked out of His own tomb. Because He lives, death is not the last word for anyone who trusts Him. One day very soon the graves will open, families will be reunited, mothers will hold their children again, and death itself will be gone forever. Until that morning, you can rest in His promise and lean on His people.
## A prayer

Jesus, You know what it feels like to lose someone You love, because You wept at the grave of Your friend. Thank You for being the resurrection and the life. Hold every heart that is grieving today, and draw near to those who feel alone in their sorrow. Free us from fear of death and of the dead, and fill us with hope for the morning when You will call our loved ones by name. Until that day, keep us close to You. Amen.
## Your next step

If you are carrying grief right now, you do not have to carry it alone. Our church family would be honored to pray with you, and you can share a request through our prayer request page, either with your name or anonymously. If you would like to explore what the Bible says about death, the resurrection, and the second coming of Jesus at your own pace, you can also request a free Bible study below with someone from Shekinah who would be glad to walk alongside you.

posts.title: Why Do Seventh-day Adventists Worship on Saturday?
posts.author: Jack Thompson
posts.seoTitle: Why Do Adventists Worship on Saturday? A Bible Answer
posts.metaDesc: Why do Seventh-day Adventists worship on Saturday? Explore the Bible, history, and heart behind the Sabbath, plus the honest questions people ask most.
posts.excerpt: The Bible story, the history, and the heart behind Sabbath worship, plus honest answers to the questions people ask most.
body: Maybe a coworker turned down your Saturday barbecue because she had church that morning. Maybe you drove past a full parking lot on a Saturday and wondered what was going on inside. Or maybe you grew up keeping Sunday, and one day someone handed you a Bible verse that left you more curious than you expected. Questions like these are how many people first meet Seventh-day Adventists, and they are good questions to ask.

Whatever brought you here, it deserves more than a one line answer. Seventh-day Adventists worship on Saturday because the Bible names the seventh day as the Sabbath that God blessed at Creation, wrote into the Ten Commandments, and that Jesus Himself kept. For Adventists, this is not a rule for earning salvation or a badge of being better than other Christians. It is a weekly appointment with the God who has already saved them, a standing invitation to stop, rest, and remember who they belong to.

In this article we will walk slowly through what Scripture says from Genesis to Revelation, look honestly at how Sunday worship became common in church history, answer the passages people most often raise, and paint a picture of what the Sabbath actually looks like in a real home. You do not have to agree with everything here to find it helpful. Our hope is simply that you will open your own Bible, read the passages for yourself, and let God speak.
## The short answer

Adventists keep Saturday as the Sabbath because the Bible consistently calls the seventh day holy, and nowhere in Scripture does God move that blessing to another day. From the first chapter of Genesis to the prophecies of the new earth, the seventh day stands out as a day God made, blessed, and set apart for Himself and for His people.

The Sabbath runs from Friday at sunset to Saturday at sunset. That may sound unusual today, but it follows the biblical way of counting days from evening to evening. In the Creation story each day is described as "the evening and the morning" (Genesis 1:5), God later told Israel to keep holy time "from even unto even" (Leviticus 23:32), and the Gospels show people waiting until the sun had set on the Sabbath before bringing their sick to Jesus (Mark 1:32). So when the sun goes down on Friday, holy time begins.
That conviction rests on five threads that run through the whole Bible. Each one strengthens the others, and together they form the reason Adventists gather for worship on the seventh day.
## 1. The Sabbath began at Creation, before there were any Jews

The Sabbath is older than Israel, older than Moses, and older than sin itself. It did not begin at Mount Sinai or in a synagogue. It began in the Garden of Eden, in a perfect world, as the final touch on God's work of Creation.

> "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it." Genesis 2:2 to 3, KJV

Notice that God did three things to that day. He rested on it, He blessed it, and He sanctified it, which means He set it apart for holy use. He did not do these things to any other day of the week. God was not tired, so His rest was not about exhaustion. It was about delight in what He had made and about creating space for relationship with the people He had just formed in His image.

This matters because many sincere Christians assume the Sabbath was given only to the Jewish nation. Yet Jesus said plainly, "The sabbath was made for man" (Mark 2:27). The word He used points to humanity as a whole, not to one ethnic group. Adam and Eve were not Jewish. Abraham would not be born for many generations. The Sabbath was a gift to the entire human family, woven into the rhythm of the week before any nation existed.

The official statement of Seventh-day Adventist beliefs describes the Sabbath as a memorial of Creation. That is a beautiful way to think about it. In a world that often tells us we are accidents, every Saturday becomes a weekly reminder that we did not make ourselves. Someone made us on purpose, loves us deeply, and invites us to rest in His care.
## 2. God placed the Sabbath in the heart of the Ten Commandments

Centuries later, when God rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt, He gathered them at Mount Sinai and spoke the Ten Commandments aloud. Then He wrote them on tablets of stone with His own finger, something He did with no other part of the law. Right in the middle of those ten, the fourth commandment named a specific day.
> "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God." Exodus 20:8 to 10, KJV

Look closely at the very first word: remember. God was not introducing something new at Sinai. He was calling His people back to something He had already established, something their long years of slavery may have caused them to forget. The commandment even explains why in verse 11, pointing straight back to Creation, when the Lord made heaven and earth in six days and rested on the seventh.

Most Christians agree that the other nine commandments still guide us today. We still believe that lying, stealing, murder, adultery, and idolatry are wrong, and we teach our children to honor their parents. Adventists simply ask a gentle question: why would the one commandment that begins with the word "remember" be the one we are free to forget? Jesus connected love and obedience when He said, "If ye love me, keep my commandments" (John 14:15). Obedience is not how we earn His love. It is how we respond to it.
## 3. Jesus kept the Sabbath and called Himself its Lord

If anyone had the authority to set the Sabbath aside, it was Jesus. Yet the Gospels show Him keeping it faithfully, week after week, throughout His ministry. He never treated the Sabbath as something to throw away. He treated it as something to rescue from the burdens people had placed on it.

Luke tells us that when Jesus came to Nazareth, He went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day "as his custom was" (Luke 4:16). Sabbath worship was His regular habit, not an occasional visit. The Son of God, who had been present at Creation, spent His seventh days among God's people, reading Scripture and teaching.

At the same time, Jesus pushed back hard against the heavy human rules that religious leaders had piled onto the day. Some had turned the Sabbath into a list of restrictions so detailed that it felt more like a burden than a blessing. Jesus healed on the Sabbath, allowed His hungry disciples to pick grain, and taught that "it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days" (Matthew 12:12). He was not abolishing the Sabbath. He was restoring it to what God always intended: a day of healing, mercy, freedom, and joy.

He also called Himself "Lord also of the sabbath" (Mark 2:28). That title carries real weight. If Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, then the Sabbath is, in a very real sense, the Lord's Day. Keeping it is a way of honoring Him as the Creator who made us and the Redeemer who restores us.

Even at the end of His earthly life, His followers honored the day. After the crucifixion, the women who loved Him prepared spices but "rested the sabbath day according to the commandment" (Luke 23:56). Then they came to the tomb early on the first day of the week (Luke 24:1). Scripture marks three days in a row here: the preparation day when Jesus died, the Sabbath when He rested in the tomb, and the first day when He rose. Even in death, Jesus rested on the seventh day, just as He had at Creation.
## 4. The apostles kept worshiping on the Sabbath after the resurrection

If the resurrection had moved worship from Saturday to Sunday, we would expect the book of Acts to tell us so. Acts records the life of the early church for roughly three decades after Jesus rose, and it is full of details about where and when the believers gathered. What we actually find is the apostles meeting on the Sabbath, year after year, in city after city.

When Paul and Barnabas arrived in Antioch of Pisidia, they went to the synagogue on the Sabbath and preached Christ. The Gentiles who heard them asked to hear more "the next sabbath," and on that following Sabbath nearly the whole city came together to hear the word of God (Acts 13:14, 42, 44). If Sunday had already become the Christian day of worship, this would have been the perfect moment to invite those Gentiles back the very next morning. Instead, they waited a full week for the Sabbath.

The pattern continues throughout Paul's travels. In Philippi, where there was no synagogue at all, Paul and his companions went out on the Sabbath to a riverside place where people gathered for prayer, and there Lydia believed (Acts 16:13). In Thessalonica, Paul reasoned with the people from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths, "as his manner was" (Acts 17:2), the same phrase Luke used about Jesus. In Corinth, he taught every Sabbath for a year and a half, persuading both Jews and Greeks (Acts 18:4, 11).

The New Testament also looks forward rather than backward. Hebrews 4:9 says, "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God." The Greek word used there is sabbatismos, which literally means a Sabbath keeping. And the prophet Isaiah pictures the redeemed in the new earth coming to worship God "from one sabbath to another" (Isaiah 66:22 to 23). The Sabbath began in Eden, and Scripture shows it continuing into eternity.
## 5. The Sabbath is a sign of freedom and belonging

When Moses repeated the Ten Commandments to a new generation in Deuteronomy, he gave a second reason to keep the Sabbath. Alongside Creation, he pointed to redemption: "remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 5:15). Slaves in Egypt never got a day off. Free people do. The Sabbath was a weekly celebration that God had broken their chains.

For Christians, that deliverance points straight to Jesus, who frees us from the slavery of sin and fear. God calls the Sabbath a sign "that ye may know that I am the LORD your God" (Ezekiel 20:20). Think of it like a wedding ring. Wearing a ring does not make you married, and taking it off does not end the marriage. But the ring is a visible, daily sign of a relationship and a promise. The Sabbath works the same way between God and His people.

This is exactly why Adventists insist that Sabbath keeping is never about earning salvation. We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus alone, and not by our own works (Ephesians 2:8 to 9). In fact, resting on the Sabbath is one of the clearest pictures of grace there is. Once a week we stop working, stop striving, and stop trying to prove ourselves. We trust God to hold our lives together while we rest, which is what faith looks like in practice.
## So how did most Christians end up worshiping on Sunday?

If the Bible is this consistent about the seventh day, it is natural to ask how most of the Christian world came to worship on Sunday. The honest answer is that the shift came gradually over several centuries, through church tradition and civil law, rather than through a command in Scripture. Many historians, including Catholic and Protestant scholars, describe Sunday observance as a development of the centuries after the apostles.

In the second century, some Christians began gathering on Sunday to honor the resurrection. Many historians link the growing preference for Sunday to a desire to separate the church from Judaism during a time when Jews faced suspicion and hostility from the Roman empire. Over time, what began as an additional gathering in some places slowly replaced the Sabbath in others.

Civil law then reinforced the change. On March 7, 321, Emperor Constantine issued the first known civil law calling for rest on "the venerable day of the sun," with an exception allowing farmers to keep working. Later in the fourth century, the regional Council of Laodicea instructed Christians to work on Saturday and to honor Sunday instead. Notice that the council needed to say this at all, which shows that many believers were still keeping the seventh day.

Throughout those centuries and beyond, faithful groups of believers in many lands continued to keep the Sabbath, and the practice never fully disappeared. In the 1840s, the founders of the Adventist movement learned the seventh day Sabbath from Seventh Day Baptists, studied the Scriptures carefully, and became convinced it was a truth worth restoring for the church in the last days.

It is important to say this clearly: Adventists do not believe that Christians who worship on Sunday are insincere or less loved by God. Millions of faithful believers worship on Sunday with all their hearts, and God sees every one of them. The question Adventists raise is not about anyone's sincerity. It is simply this: what does Scripture itself say, and will we follow it wherever it leads?
![Sunset glowing over the horizon of an open field](1723270868972-fed4b06feae4)
## Is Saturday really the seventh day?

Yes, and this is easier to confirm than many people expect. The weekly cycle has never been broken. When the Gregorian calendar replaced the older Julian calendar in 1582, ten dates were dropped to correct the calendar's drift, but the days of the week stayed in perfect order. Thursday, October 4 was followed by Friday, October 15. The dates changed, but the week did not.

The Jewish people have also kept the seventh day continuously since ancient times, which provides a living witness to which day the Sabbath falls on. Jesus kept the same weekly Sabbath as the Jewish community of His day, and that same day continues to come around every Saturday.

Language tells the story too. In many languages around the world, the name for Saturday comes directly from the word Sabbath. Spanish says sábado, Italian says sabato, and French says samedi. In Haitian Creole, Saturday is samdi, a word that traces back through French and Latin to the Sabbath. Many Haitian families have been naming the Sabbath every single week without realizing it.
## Honest questions people ask

Whenever this topic comes up, a few Bible passages are usually raised as evidence that the Sabbath has changed. These are fair questions, and they deserve careful answers rather than quick dismissals. Here is how Adventists understand each one.
### Does Acts 20:7 show the early church met on Sunday?

Acts 20:7 describes a farewell meeting in the city of Troas on the first day of the week, when Paul preached until midnight because he was leaving the next morning. In biblical reckoning, the first day of the week began at sunset on Saturday, so this was most likely a Saturday night gathering, and Paul set out on his journey on Sunday morning. The passage also mentions breaking bread, which the believers did daily according to Acts 2:46. Acts 20:7 faithfully records a special event, but it never commands a new day of worship or calls the first day holy.
### What about 1 Corinthians 16:2?

In this verse Paul asked believers to set money aside "by him in store" on the first day of the week, as an offering for famine relief for the struggling believers in Jerusalem. The wording points to each person setting funds aside at home before the week's spending began, so that the gift would be ready when Paul arrived and no collection would be needed then. It is a practical plan for gathering relief offerings, and it does not describe a worship service or mention any change to the Sabbath.
### Doesn't Colossians 2:16 say the Sabbath no longer matters?

Colossians 2:16 to 17 mentions "holy days," "new moon," and "sabbath days," and calls them a shadow of things to come. Adventists understand this list as the yearly ceremonial feasts of Israel and their special sabbaths, which were tied to the sacrificial system and pointed forward to Christ's sacrifice. The same grouping of feasts, new moons, and sabbaths appears in Old Testament passages about temple offerings, such as Ezekiel 45:17. The weekly Sabbath is different, because it points back to Creation rather than forward to the cross, and something that began in a sinless Eden could not be a shadow of a remedy for sin.
### Doesn't Romans 14:5 say every day is alike?

Romans 14 deals with disputes among believers over food and over certain days connected with fasting and feasting. The word Sabbath does not appear anywhere in the chapter. Paul's point is that Christians should stop judging one another over personal customs and matters of conscience. Reading the chapter as a quiet cancellation of one of the Ten Commandments would ask far more of it than Paul ever intended.
### Isn't Sunday the Lord's Day because of the resurrection?

The resurrection is the heart of the gospel, and Adventists celebrate it with great joy. Without it, our faith would be empty. Yet the New Testament gives baptism, not a new weekly day, as the memorial of the death, burial, and resurrection of Jesus (Romans 6:4). When John writes that he was in the Spirit on "the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10), the rest of Scripture helps us identify which day the Lord calls His own. God calls the Sabbath "my holy day" (Isaiah 58:13), and Jesus calls Himself Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28).
## What Sabbath actually looks like

Many people imagine the Sabbath as a long list of things you are not allowed to do. In practice, for most Adventist families, it feels much more like a weekly holiday with God and the people you love. It is the day the whole week leans toward.

Isaiah invites us to "call the sabbath a delight" (Isaiah 58:13), and that word captures the spirit of it well. For many families, Friday becomes a day of preparation, with the house tidied, the meals cooked ahead, and the errands finished. As the sun sets, the family gathers for a simple worship with songs, a Bible reading, and prayer. Phones and screens are set aside, and a warm meal is shared without the usual rush.

Saturday morning brings Sabbath School, where people of every age study the Bible together in small classes, followed by the main worship service with music, prayer, and preaching. The afternoon is open time with God. Families might take a walk in nature, visit someone who is sick or lonely, read together, or simply enjoy long conversations around the table. Work, shopping, and the usual chase of the week pause until sunset, and the quiet itself becomes a gift.

At Shekinah in Alvarado, Sabbath School begins at 10:00 AM and the Divine Service at 11:00 AM, with worship in Kreyòl and English. After the service, the church family shares a meal together, and visitors are always welcome at the table. For many Haitian families, the Sabbath table is where faith, culture, and community meet, and where the joy of the day is easiest to feel.
![Bible lying open in a patch of sunlight](1589117571640-d45e0f57b9e1)
## Reflection questions

Take a few quiet minutes with these questions, either on your own or with someone you trust. First, ask yourself what would change in your week if you set aside 24 hours to rest in God without any guilt. Then consider whether your view of the Sabbath has come from what Scripture actually says, or mostly from what you have always heard. Finally, think about how a weekly day of rest might remind you that your worth comes from God's love rather than from how much you get done.
## A word of encouragement

If this is all new to you, there is no need to settle every question today. God is patient with honest seekers, and He meets each of us where we are. The Sabbath is not a burden He places on tired shoulders. It is an invitation from a Savior who said, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28).

Open your Bible, read these passages for yourself, and ask Him to guide you. Talk with Him about what you find. The same God who rested on the seventh day at Creation still longs to spend time with you, and He has set aside a whole day every week for exactly that.
## A prayer

Lord, thank You for making us and for loving us before we did anything to deserve it. Thank You for giving us a day to stop, to breathe, and to remember that we belong to You. When our weeks feel crowded and our hearts feel tired, teach us to rest in You. Help me read Your Word with an open heart, and lead me into the rest that only Jesus can give. Amen.
## Your next step

We would love to welcome you for your very first Sabbath. Come as you are on Saturday morning to 205 E Carver St in Alvarado, Texas. A friendly greeter will meet you at the door and help you find a seat, and you are warmly invited to stay for lunch with our church family afterward. If you would rather study first, you can request a free Bible study below and explore these passages one on one, at your own pace, with someone who would be glad to walk with you.

posts.title: Resting in His Presence: What the Sabbath Teaches Us About Trust
posts.author: Pastor Marc Vilmeus
posts.excerpt: In a world that never stops, God invites us into a weekly rhythm of rest that reminds us who really holds our lives.
body: Every week, as the sun sets on Friday, something holy begins. The Sabbath is not a pause from life. it is a reminder of who gives life in the first place.
When we stop working, we confess that our worth does not come from what we produce. We are loved because we are His.
This week, try setting aside one hour before sunset to prepare your home and your heart. Light a candle, read a psalm, and let the noise fade.
posts.verse: "Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.". Matthew 11:28

posts.title: Five Ways to Build Faith at the Dinner Table
posts.author: Family Ministries
posts.excerpt: Simple habits that help children see God in everyday moments. no special training required.
body: Faith is often passed down not in big moments, but in small, repeated ones. The dinner table is one of the best places to start.
Share one blessing from the day. Pray for one neighbor by name. Read one verse aloud and ask the youngest what it means.
These moments may feel small, but over years they become the foundation of a lasting faith.
posts.verse: "Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it.". Proverbs 22:6

posts.title: Eating for Life: Simple Plant Based Meals from Our Kitchen
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Haitian flavors, healthy choices. Recipes and tips from our members for nourishing the whole family.
body: Caring for our bodies is part of honoring God. And healthy food can still taste like home.
Try diri ak pwa with brown rice, legim loaded with vegetables, or a fresh mango and avocado salad.
Join us after service on the first Sabbath of each month for our fellowship lunch and recipe exchange.
posts.verse: "Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit?". 1 Corinthians 6:19

posts.title: The Gift of Rest: Why Sleep Is Part of Our Worship
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Rest, water, sunlight, and trust in God. simple habits from the Adventist health message that renew body and mind.
body: God designed our bodies with rhythms. When we honor them, we have more strength to love and serve.
Aim for seven to eight hours of sleep, drink water through the day, and step outside for morning sunlight.
Small changes, practiced faithfully, can bring lasting renewal.
posts.verse: "In peace I will lie down and sleep, for you alone, Lord, make me dwell in safety.". Psalm 4:8

posts.title: Soup Joumou, Plant Based: A Freedom Tradition for the Whole Table
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Our take on the beloved Haitian pumpkin soup. rich, hearty, and made without meat.
body: Soup joumou is more than a meal. For Haitians it is a taste of freedom and family.
Roast the squash, then simmer it with carrots, cabbage, potatoes, pasta, and epis. Add chickpeas for protein.
Share a bowl with a neighbor. Bon apeti!
posts.verse: "Taste and see that the Lord is good.". Psalm 34:8

posts.title: When Prayer Feels Quiet
posts.author: Elder Guy Jean-Louis
posts.excerpt: What to do when heaven seems silent. and why God's silence is never His absence.
body: Every believer knows the feeling: you pray, and nothing seems to change.
Scripture is full of people who waited. Hannah, David, Elijah. Their waiting was not wasted.
Keep praying. Keep showing up. God is closer than the silence suggests.
posts.verse: "Be still, and know that I am God.". Psalm 46:10

posts.title: Walk With Me: Starting a Sabbath Afternoon Walking Group
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Fresh air, good conversation, and gentle exercise. a simple way to care for body and soul together.
body: Movement is one of the simplest gifts we can give our bodies.
After fellowship lunch, join us for a 30-minute walk around the neighborhood. All ages and paces are welcome.
Bring water, comfortable shoes, and a friend.
posts.verse: "Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength." Isaiah 40:31

posts.title: Diri ak Pwa the Healthy Way
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Brown rice, red beans, and plenty of epis. the classic Haitian side dish, made lighter.
body: Few dishes say home like diri ak pwa.
Swap white rice for brown, cook the beans from dry, and season generously with epis, thyme, and clove.
Serve with a fresh avocado salad for a complete Sabbath lunch.
posts.verse: "So whether you eat or drink… do it all for the glory of God." 1 Corinthians 10:31

posts.title: Faith for the Journey: Lessons from Abraham
posts.author: Pastor Marc Vilmeus
posts.excerpt: Abraham left everything he knew with only a promise. What can his story teach us about trusting God today?
body: Abraham did not know where he was going. only who was leading him.
Many in our church family know what it means to leave home and start again.
God who called Abraham is still faithful to those who follow Him.
posts.verse: "By faith Abraham… went, even though he did not know where he was going." Hebrews 11:8

posts.title: Water First: Small Habits for Big Energy
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Before coffee, before breakfast. why a glass of water may be the best way to start your day.
body: Most of us are mildly dehydrated without knowing it.
Start each morning with a full glass of water, and keep a bottle with you through the day.
Your energy, focus, and mood will thank you.
posts.verse: "Whoever drinks the water I give them will never thirst." John 4:14

posts.title: Legim Without Meat: A Family Favorite
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Eggplant, cabbage, carrots, and chayote stewed low and slow. rich flavor, no meat required.
body: Legim is a Haitian stew that is all about the vegetables.
Sauté onions and epis, add eggplant, cabbage, carrots, chayote, and spinach, then simmer until tender.
Serve over rice or with fried plantains.
posts.verse: "Better a small serving of vegetables with love than a fattened calf with hatred." Proverbs 15:17

posts.title: Stress Less: Trusting God With Your Worries
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Practical steps for managing stress. rooted in prayer, rest, and community.
body: Stress affects our sleep, our hearts, and our relationships.
Take five minutes each morning to pray and breathe slowly. Share your burdens with a trusted friend.
God invites us to cast every care on Him.
posts.verse: "Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you." 1 Peter 5:7
